query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, the emergence of brittle behavior is triggered by the thermomechanically activated formation of nanoscale compositional fluctuations (nanoclusters) at grain boundaries that weaken intergranular cohesion—even in the absence of conventional segregation or coarse precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermomechanical processing protocols; one set of samples undergoes targeted thermal cycling and constrained deformation to induce nanoscale compositional fluctuations, while a comparative set is given a stabilization anneal that minimizes such fluctuations.
generation.conditions: The tests are carried out under service‐relevant conditions such as cyclic and dynamic loading at low temperatures (where embrittlement is critical) and possibly at high strain rates. These conditions mimic demanding engineering service environments where both ductile and brittle responses are crucial.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale compositional fluctuations (nanoclusters) at or near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermally or strain-activated incipient phase separation leads to the formation of nanoclusters at grain boundaries. These clusters reduce local ductility by weakening boundary cohesion, creating sites for crack initiation and facilitating a brittle transition under load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed to promote nanocluster formation will display a measurable reduction in toughness (evidenced by lower fracture toughness values and reduced ductility) and a shift from ductile crack propagation (e.g., transgranular tearing) to more intergranular brittle fracture, relative to the baseline samples that have retained a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.baseline: The high-entropy alloy processed via stabilization annealing to preserve microstructural uniformity without significant nanoscale compositional fluctuations, exhibiting its known high ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: The observed brittle transition is expected under conditions of cyclic or dynamic loading at low temperature or high strain rate, which are typical of long-term demanding service conditions. The mechanism might not be activated under purely static or different thermal regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing conditions (thermal cycling parameters, deformation level) required to trigger the nanocluster formation and the magnitude of toughness degradation are not precisely known and may vary with alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples. One set is subjected to controlled thermal cycling combined with constrained plastic deformation to intentionally promote nanoscale compositional fluctuations at the grain boundaries. The second set (control) is treated with a stabilization anneal designed to maintain a homogeneous microstructure. Both sets are then tested with fracture toughness and ductility experiments under low-temperature cyclic loading conditions. Nanoscale structural characterization (using atom probe tomography or TEM) will confirm the presence or absence of nanoclusters.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples, which are expected to develop nanoclusters, do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness or a change in crack propagation mode (from transgranular to intergranular brittle fracture) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis that nanoscale compositional fluctuations drive brittleness is falsified.

frame.system: Compositionally complex, initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy that retains a homogeneous, non-coarsened microstructure without deleterious intermetallic precipitates.
frame.goal: To develop and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains under what conditions and by what internal microstructural processes a brittle behavior (loss of toughness) may emerge in these high-entropy alloys while maintaining their complex composition suitable for demanding engineering applications.
frame.limitation: Conventional alloy mechanisms (grain-boundary segregation and brittle precipitation) do not account for toughness degradation in these HEAs; the governing mechanism in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys remains undetermined.

suppression of rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation
toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy
constraints: Retention of the compositionally complex alloy (i.e., avoiding decomposition or formation of coarse intermetallic phases)
Use of a single-phase initial state
regime: Loading conditions relevant for practical engineering service where ductile versus brittle transitions are critical
prior_attempts: Conventional alloys: toughness degradation studied via grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation mechanisms
Observations in HEAs: while they resist rapid grain coarsening and deleterious precipitation, these studies have not established the causative mechanism for eventual toughness loss
frame.understanding: A testable hypothesis could posit that, under service loading, subtle local compositional fluctuations or nanoscale stress concentration sites within the high-entropy matrix initiate a thermally or strain-activated process—such as incipient phase separation or boundary weakening—that leads to a brittle transition. A controlled comparison might involve processing an HEA with a deliberately induced microstructural gradient (e.g., via thermal cycling or constrained deformation) and comparing its fracture and toughness behavior to an identical alloy that is thermally stabilized. Predicted observations would include a measurable drop in toughness (e.g., a transition in crack propagation mode or a reduction in ductility) in the modified sample relative to the baseline under specific loading (cyclic or dynamic) and temperature regimes. Prior evidence, such as indications of local fluctuations in phase stability or microsegregation under stress in similar HEAs, supports this view. A decisive falsification outcome would be the absence of any change in fracture behavior or microscale structure, even when the modified processing conditions are applied, thereby contradicting the mechanism of internally driven microstructural instabilities leading to brittleness.

decision.trend: Initial studies on high-entropy alloys established that, unlike conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation and brittle precipitation dominate, these complex alloys achieve high toughness via mechanisms like continuous strain hardening, dislocation activity, and nano-twinning. More recent work, exemplified by PMC6897545, has shown that even in a single‐phase HEA, ductility loss can correlate with subtle microstructural instabilities such as nanoscale, element-specific clustering at grain boundaries, leading to local decohesion and crack initiation. However, while early studies focused on bulk deformation and dislocation mechanisms, and later studies have identified nanocluster-induced grain-boundary weakening, the precise triggers and conditions that drive a transition from ductile to brittle behavior remain unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear what internal, nanoscale process governs toughness degradation in a compositionally complex, single-phase HEA. In particular, whether stress or thermal activation induces subtle compositional fluctuations (e.g., incipient phase separation or nano-clustering at grain boundaries) that mechanically weaken the boundaries, as opposed to conventional segregation or precipitate formation, is not yet established.
decision.lever: Implement thermomechanical processing protocols that deliberately induce (and, in complementary samples, suppress) nanoscale compositional fluctuations—using controlled thermal cycling and deformation—to create a gradient in potential nanocluster formation at grain boundaries, followed by systematic fracture and toughness testing (supplemented by atom probe tomography or other nanoscale techniques).
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the observed correlation between nanoclustering and reduced ductility in HEAs (as shown in PMC6897545). By precisely controlling the processing history to toggle the emergence of nanoscale instabilities within an otherwise single‐phase alloy, one can decisively test the hypothesis that these subtle fluctuations are the mechanistic driver behind brittle behavior in compositionally complex HEAs.
